title: Law, regulation, governance and human rights
blurb: Tell statute from case law and guidance, know who regulates whom across the UK, and apply human rights and mandatory reporting duties.
question: A nurse in an English sexual health clinic examines Amina, 15, and sees physical signs that female genital mutilation has been carried out. Amina says it happened years ago abroad. What must the nurse do?

teach.body: Nursing practice is governed by four layers. Statute: Acts of Parliament such as the Mental Capacity Act 2005, Care Act 2014 and Human Rights Act 1998. Common law: judges' decisions, such as Montgomery (2015) on consent. Guidance: NICE and national policy, which is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account. Professional standards: the NMC Code. Proficiency P1.2 asks you to understand and apply all of these, including mandatory reporting duties.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P1.2, P7.2

teach.caption: NICE guidance is not mandatory, but professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside the person's needs and preferences.
Nurses and midwives are registered UK-wide; nursing associates are regulated in England only.

head: Nation
Capacity law
Care regulator
teach.caption: Code 4.3: keep to the mental capacity law of the country in which you are practising.

Right
Practice example
rows: No torture, inhuman or degrading treatment
teach.caption: HRA s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right.

teach.h: Tracey: talk to people about DNACPR
teach.body: In R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals (2014), the Court of Appeal held that Article 8 is engaged by decisions about DNACPR. There is a presumption that the patient will be consulted before a DNACPR notice is placed, unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation being likely to cause physical or psychological harm. Not wanting to upset someone is not, by itself, that reason.
teach.cite: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS FT [2014] EWCA Civ 822

steps.label: Discover
steps.sub: Girl under 18 tells you, or you see physical signs

steps.label: Within one month
steps.sub: Of first discovering it; orally or in writing

teach.caption: FGM Act 2003 s5B: regulated health professionals must notify the police. The disclosure does not breach confidence.

teach.body: Amina is 15, and the nurse sees physical signs of FGM. Because she is under 18 and the nurse is a regulated health professional working in England, s5B of the FGM Act 2003 requires the nurse to notify the police within one month. It does not matter that it happened abroad or years ago. The disclosure does not breach confidentiality. The nurse also follows safeguarding procedures and explains to Amina, sensitively, what will happen.

teach.text: The FGM duty is personal and specific: girls UNDER 18, KNOWN cases (disclosed or physical signs seen), reported to the POLICE. For a woman aged 18 or over, or a girl only thought to be at risk, use safeguarding procedures instead. And don't confuse the CQC (regulates organisations in England) with the NMC (regulates you).

items: Statute, common law, professional standards and guidance all shape practice; NICE guidance is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account.
NMC regulates individual registrants; CQC regulates providers in England (HIW Wales, HIS Scotland, RQIA Northern Ireland).
Capacity law is devolved: MCA 2005 (England and Wales), AWI 2000 (Scotland), MCA (NI) 2016.
HRA Articles 2, 3, 5, 8, 9 and 14; Tracey means consult before DNACPR unless it would cause harm.
Mandatory reporting: FGM in under-18s to police within a month; tell the NMC about charges or cautions (Code 23.2).

summary: You can now tell statute from case law, guidance and professional standards, name the right regulator in each UK nation, and link common situations to Human Rights Act articles. You also know the specific mandatory reporting duties, including FGM in under-18s.

A.q: During induction, a colleague tells Grace that one organisation keeps the register, publishes the Code and decides fitness to practise cases about individual nurses. Which organisation is this?
options: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Royal College of Nursing
The Department of Health and Social Care
A.why: The NMC is the professional regulator for nurses, midwives and nursing associates: it keeps the register, sets the Code and handles fitness to practise (Code 2015, updated 2018).

whyNot.0: The CQC regulates registered providers in England, not individual nurses.
whyNot.2: The RCN is a professional body and trade union without regulatory powers.
whyNot.3: The DHSC sets health policy but does not register nurses.

A.q: Mr Rahman, 58, is a practising Muslim on a surgical ward. He asks for help to pray at set times. Which Human Rights Act article most directly applies?
options: Article 8, respect for private and family life, home and correspondence
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
A.why: Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including manifesting religion in worship and practice (HRA 1998 Sch 1).

whyNot.0: Article 8 covers privacy and family life; religious practice falls more directly under Article 9.
whyNot.1: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of other rights; it is not the primary right here.
whyNot.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not religious practice.

A.q: A student asks what legal status a NICE guideline has for registered nurses. Which answer is most accurate?
options: It is a statutory instrument that every nurse must follow in full detail
It is case law created when NICE defends a claim in court
It is optional advice that a trust may choose to adopt
It is guidance to take fully into account with the person's needs
A.why: NICE's standard 'Your responsibility' statement: guidance is not mandatory, but professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside individual needs, preferences and values.

whyNot.1: NICE guidance is not created by court judgments.
whyNot.2: It is more than optional: it should be taken fully into account in clinical decisions.

B.q: Grace has worked as a nurse in Manchester and is moving to Glasgow. Which statute will govern decisions for adults who lack capacity in her new post?
options: Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000
Mental Capacity Act 2005
Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016
Care Act 2014 with Scottish guidance
B.why: Capacity law is devolved. In Scotland, decisions for adults lacking capacity fall under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Code 4.3: keep to the capacity law of the country where you practise.

whyNot.1: The MCA 2005 applies in England and Wales.
whyNot.2: The 2016 Act applies in Northern Ireland.
whyNot.3: The Care Act 2014 is English social care law and is not capacity law.

B.q: Mrs Ellis, 81, has advanced heart failure and full capacity. A doctor completes a DNACPR form overnight and asks the nurse not to mention it because it might upset her. What does Tracey (2014) indicate?
options: Her daughter should be told instead, as her next of kin
Clinicians may decide this without telling her, because CPR is purely a medical decision
She should be consulted unless this would cause her physical or psychological harm
The form is invalid until she has signed it herself in front of a witness
B.why: Tracey held that Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions, with a presumption of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as likely physical or psychological harm. Possible upset is not enough.

whyNot.0: Mrs Ellis has capacity, so she, not her family, should be consulted.
whyNot.1: Tracey requires consultation; not discussing it to avoid upset is not a convincing reason.
whyNot.3: A DNACPR decision does not require the patient's signature or a witness to be valid.

B.q: On a ward in England, Mr Hughes, 70, receives a tenfold insulin overdose and needs transfer to intensive care. Which body regulates the trust's statutory duty of candour?
options: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Health and Safety Executive
The General Medical Council
The Care Quality Commission
B.why: The statutory duty of candour (reg 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014) applies to registered providers and is regulated by the CQC in England.

whyNot.0: The NMC oversees the professional duty of candour for individual registrants (Code 14).
whyNot.1: The HSE enforces workplace health and safety law such as RIDDOR, not reg 20.
whyNot.2: The GMC oversees doctors' professional duty, not the provider's statutory duty.

C.q: In an English sexual health clinic, Amina, 15, has physical signs of female genital mutilation. She says it was done years ago abroad. What must the nurse do?
options: Notify the police herself, within one month of discovering it
Record it and refer to the GP, as it happened outside the UK
Ask Amina's consent before telling anyone outside the clinic
Pass the information to the safeguarding lead so they can report it
C.why: FGM Act 2003 s5B: a regulated health professional in England or Wales who discovers FGM in a girl under 18 must notify the police within one month. The disclosure does not breach confidence. Safeguarding procedures are followed as well.

whyNot.1: Where and when it was done does not remove the reporting duty.
whyNot.2: The duty applies whether or not she consents, and disclosure does not breach confidence.
whyNot.3: The duty is personal to the professional who discovers it; safeguarding referral is in addition.

C.q: Nurse Kemi is cautioned by police for a minor offence outside work. Her manager suggests she need not mention it because it was not work-related. What does the Code require?
options: Declare it to the NMC at her next revalidation in three years
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Declare it to the NMC if it results in a court conviction
C.why: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and your employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge, conditional discharge or conviction (other than a protected caution or conviction).

whyNot.0: Waiting until revalidation does not meet 'as soon as you can'.
whyNot.2: The duty to tell the NMC is the nurse's own.
whyNot.3: A caution must be declared, not only convictions.

C.q: A care home resident lacks capacity, and staff lock the front door and stop her going out. Which Human Rights Act article is most directly engaged?
options: Article 2, the right to life
Article 9, freedom of religion
Article 5, liberty and security
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
C.why: Article 5 protects the right to liberty and requires lawful procedures for any deprivation of liberty; the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards exist to provide them for people who lack capacity.

whyNot.0: Article 2 concerns the right to life, not restriction of movement.
whyNot.1: Article 9 concerns thought, conscience and religion.
whyNot.3: Article 14 protects against discrimination in enjoying other rights and is not the primary right engaged.

reteach.title: Ask three questions: what kind of rule, whose rule, which country?
reteach.question: Faced with any legal question in the exam, which three questions sort it out?

blocks.body: What KIND of rule is it? An Act (statute) binds; a judgment (case law) binds; the Code sets professional standards; NICE guidance must be taken fully into account. WHOSE duty is it? Yours (Code, FGM reporting, telling the NMC about a caution) or the organisation's (statutory candour, CQC registration)? Which COUNTRY? Capacity law and regulators differ across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

blocks.text: Montgomery is common law (a Supreme Court judgment); the MCA 2005 is statute; the Code is a professional standard.

explain.body: Statute is made by Parliament (MCA 2005, Care Act 2014, HRA 1998). Common law comes from court judgments (Montgomery 2015, Tracey 2014). The Code is a professional standard; NICE is guidance to take fully into account.

test.q: Which of these is common law rather than statute?
options: The Human Rights Act 1998
The Mental Capacity Act 2005
Montgomery v Lanarkshire
The Care Act 2014
test.why: Montgomery is a UK Supreme Court judgment, so it is common (case) law.

whyNot.0: The HRA is an Act of Parliament.
whyNot.1: The MCA is an Act of Parliament.
whyNot.3: The Care Act is an Act of Parliament.

explain.body: The NMC regulates individual nurses, midwives and nursing associates. Care providers are regulated by the CQC in England, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, Healthcare Improvement Scotland and the RQIA in Northern Ireland.

test.q: Which body inspects NHS services and regulates independent healthcare in Wales?
options: The Care Quality Commission
Healthcare Inspectorate Wales
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The RQIA
test.why: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales is the independent regulator of healthcare and inspectorate of NHS services in Wales.

whyNot.0: The CQC regulates providers in England.
whyNot.2: The NMC regulates individual registrants UK-wide, not services.

explain.body: Public authorities must act compatibly with Convention rights (HRA s6). Key articles: 2 life, 3 no inhuman or degrading treatment, 5 liberty, 8 private and family life, 9 religion, 14 no discrimination.

test.q: A patient is left exposed in a corridor while waiting for a commode. Which article is most engaged?
options: Article 3, inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 9, freedom of thought and religion
Article 2, the right to life
test.why: Treatment that humiliates and undermines dignity engages Article 3 (and privacy under Article 8).

explain.body: Some duties are fixed by law: FGM in girls under 18 must be reported to the police within one month (FGM Act 2003 s5B); notifiable diseases are notified on clinical suspicion; cautions and charges must be declared to the NMC (Code 23.2).

test.q: Which situation triggers the FGM mandatory reporting duty to the police?
options: A woman aged 24 discloses FGM in childhood
A girl of 16 discloses FGM done when she was 9
A mother says her daughter may be taken abroad
A girl of 12 is thought to be at risk of FGM
test.why: The duty applies where a girl under 18 discloses FGM, or signs are seen, whenever it was done (FGM Act 2003 s5B).

whyNot.0: She is over 18, so the mandatory police duty does not apply; offer support and follow safeguarding procedures.
whyNot.2: Risk without a known case is handled through safeguarding procedures.
whyNot.3: Suspected risk is a safeguarding matter, not a mandatory police report.
